What happens when a T. rex wakes up in downtown Tokyo? How long would a house cat last in the Late Jurassic?

Era Swap is a what-if science series about animals out of their time. Every episode takes one creature, sends it to an age it was never built for, and starts a timer. Prehistoric giants come forward into our cities, oceans and farms. Modern pets and wildlife go back to meet the dinosaurs. Then we watch what breaks first: the air, the food, the weather, or the neighbours.

The trips are imaginary, the science is not. Body sizes, temperatures, oxygen levels and who eats whom come from fossils and real research, and when scientists simply don't know, we say so.

Coming up: megalodons, mammoths, sabre-toothed cats, house cats, golden retrievers and one very confused goldfish.

Subscribe and place your bets: who makes it to the end of the clock?

chi_tiet.tieu_de: How Long Would Ice Age Giants Survive in Today's World
chi_tiet.mo_ta:
How long would Ice Age giants survive in today's world? Six of them wake up back where they once lived, as those places are now: a woolly rhino in Siberia, a giant short-faced bear in Alaska, a woolly mammoth on Wrangel Island, Megalania in Queensland, a Megatherium in Argentina and a giant deer in Ireland. Each one gets a clock. Their world only ended about 12,000 years ago, so how different could it be? Five of the clocks stop. One is still running at the end.

Real places, real fossils, real records. The giants waking up is the only made-up part, and where the evidence runs out, we say it's our guess.

chi_tiet.tieu_de: How Long Would Prehistoric Sky Monsters Survive in Today's World
chi_tiet.mo_ta:
How long would prehistoric sky monsters survive in today's world? 

Eight of them wake up back where their bones were found, as those places are now: Hatzegopteryx in a hay field in Transylvania; Dimorphodon on the seafront at Lyme Regis; Pteranodon in the wheat fields of Kansas; Rhamphorhynchus over the Altmühl river in Bavaria; Argentavis on the flat pampas of Argentina; Tupandactylus in the dry hills of north-east Brazil; Cryodrakon on the Alberta prairie; and Pelagornis on an airport runway in Charleston. 

Each one gets a clock. When it stops, the next one wakes up. They can all fly, so this should be easy: don't like where you landed, fly somewhere else. Only one of the eight is still flying at the end.

Real places, real animals that live there today, real records. The only made-up part is the monsters waking up.
